facts.fact: People are more likely to comply with a request if they're given a reason for it, even if the reason is fairly weak.
Humans tend to mimic the body language, speech patterns, and expressions of people they're comfortable with, a phenomenon called the chameleon effect.
People consistently overestimate how much others are paying attention to them, a bias known as the spotlight effect.
When a group is asked to make a decision together, individual members often become less cautious than they would be alone, a shift called group polarization.
The mere presence of other people can improve performance on simple, well-practiced tasks and hurt performance on complex, unfamiliar ones.
People tend to rate their own abilities as above average across nearly every skill, a pattern known as illusory superiority.
Waiting in an unexplained line feels far more frustrating than waiting the same amount of time when you know the reason for the delay.
People are more likely to help a stranger in an emergency when they are the only witness than when many other people are present, a pattern called the bystander effect.
Small initial commitments make people far more likely to agree to larger requests later, a pattern called the foot-in-the-door effect.
Humans are wired to notice and remember negative experiences more strongly than positive ones, a tendency called negativity bias.
People often judge the likelihood of an event based on how easily examples come to mind, rather than actual statistics — this is the availability heuristic.
Offering too many choices can leave people less satisfied with their final decision than offering just a few, a pattern known as choice overload.
People tend to conform to group opinions even when they privately believe the group is wrong, as shown in classic conformity experiments.
Once someone commits to a decision, even a bad one, they tend to justify it rather than admit it was a mistake — a pattern known as commitment bias.
People are more persuaded by stories and personal anecdotes than by statistics, even when the statistics are more reliable.
Chronic stress can physically shrink areas of the brain involved in memory and emotional regulation over time.
Regular physical exercise has been shown to reduce symptoms of mild to moderate depression about as effectively as some forms of therapy.
Writing about a stressful experience for just a few minutes a day can measurably reduce anxiety and improve mood over time.
Social isolation is linked to health risks comparable to smoking or obesity, according to long-term health research.
Naming an emotion out loud, a practice called affect labeling, can reduce its intensity by activating regulation centers in the brain.
Sleep deprivation increases activity in the brain's threat-detection center, making people more likely to react to neutral situations as if they were negative.
People with a strong sense of purpose tend to report higher life satisfaction, even when facing significant hardship.
Spending time in nature has been linked to lower activity in brain regions associated with rumination and negative self-focus.
Perfectionism is more strongly linked to anxiety and burnout than it is to actual achievement.
Gratitude practices, like writing down three good things each day, are associated with measurable increases in wellbeing over several weeks.
Emotional suppression often backfires, increasing the physiological stress response instead of calming it.
Having at least one close, trusted relationship is one of the strongest predictors of long-term emotional resilience.
Excessive social media use has been associated with increased feelings of loneliness, especially with passive scrolling rather than active interaction.
Deep, slow breathing directly activates the parasympathetic nervous system, physically lowering heart rate and stress hormones.
Self-compassion, treating yourself the way you'd treat a friend, is linked to lower anxiety than self-criticism, even when both come from a wish to improve.
The human brain uses about 20 percent of the body's total energy despite making up only around 2 percent of its weight.
New neural connections can form throughout life, a property called neuroplasticity, even into old age.
The brain processes visual information faster than any other sense, which is part of why images are remembered better than text.
Short-term memory can typically hold only about four to seven pieces of information at once before older items get pushed out.
The brain consolidates memories most effectively during deep sleep, which is one reason sleep loss impairs learning.
Multitasking usually isn't true simultaneous processing — the brain rapidly switches attention between tasks, which slows both down.
Dopamine is released in anticipation of a reward, not just after receiving it, which is part of why anticipation itself feels pleasurable.
The left and right hemispheres of the brain communicate constantly through a thick bundle of nerve fibers called the corpus callosum.
The brain often fills in gaps in visual information without you noticing, which is why optical illusions can trick perception so easily.
Chronic multitasking with digital devices has been linked to reduced attention span and weaker working memory over time.
The prefrontal cortex, responsible for planning and impulse control, doesn't fully mature until the mid-20s.
Learning a new skill physically changes the brain's structure, thickening the regions used most during practice.
The brain can't multitask on complex cognitive work the way it can on physical tasks like walking and talking at the same time.
Mirror neurons fire both when you perform an action and when you watch someone else perform it, which may underlie empathy.
The hippocampus, key to forming new memories, is one of the few brain regions that can grow new neurons in adulthood.
People are more likely to feel attracted to someone after going through a mildly stressful or exciting experience together, an effect linked to misattribution of arousal.
Similarity in values and habits predicts long-term relationship satisfaction more reliably than similarity in interests or hobbies.
Couples who express gratitude toward each other regularly report significantly higher relationship satisfaction over time.
Eye contact can increase feelings of closeness and attraction between two people faster than conversation alone.
The brain's reward system activates in early romantic love in patterns that resemble the activity seen with addictive substances.
Proximity and repeated exposure to someone tend to increase liking, an effect known as the mere exposure effect.
Couples who argue constructively, focusing on the issue rather than character attacks, tend to have more stable long-term relationships.
People often unconsciously seek partners whose personality traits complement, rather than simply mirror, their own.
Physical touch, like a hug, can lower cortisol and raise oxytocin levels, strengthening feelings of bonding and trust.
How a couple responds to each other's good news predicts relationship satisfaction even more strongly than how they handle conflict.
Long-distance couples often report higher levels of intimacy in conversation, since physical distance pushes communication to become more intentional.
First impressions of attraction can form within milliseconds, well before any conscious evaluation takes place.
Shared laughter between partners is strongly associated with feelings of closeness and relationship satisfaction.
People tend to be more attracted to faces that are close to an averaged composite of many faces, which the brain reads as familiar and trustworthy.
Attachment styles formed in early childhood often shape patterns of trust and closeness in adult romantic relationships.
The Big Five personality traits — openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism — remain fairly stable but can shift gradually across a lifetime.
Introverts and extroverts differ in how they process stimulation, with extroverts generally needing more external input to feel alert.
People high in conscientiousness tend to live longer on average, partly due to healthier habits and more consistent routines.
Personality can appear to shift depending on context — a person may act more extroverted at work and more reserved at home.
High openness to experience is associated with greater creativity and a stronger interest in novel ideas and perspectives.
People with high emotional stability tend to recover from stressful events more quickly than those high in neuroticism.
Traits like humor and warmth are consistently rated as more attractive over time than traits like status or wealth.
Handwriting analysis, or graphology, has not been scientifically validated as a reliable indicator of personality.
Personality traits tend to become more stable with age, generally settling into consistent patterns by the 30s.
People high in agreeableness tend to prioritize group harmony, sometimes at the cost of expressing their own needs.
Birth order has a much smaller effect on personality than popular belief suggests, according to large-scale studies.
Self-monitoring, the ability to adjust behavior to social context, varies significantly between individuals and affects how adaptable someone seems socially.
People tend to unconsciously seek environments and relationships that reinforce their existing personality traits.
A person's personality can predict career satisfaction more reliably than intelligence alone.
Highly sensitive people process sensory and emotional information more deeply, which can mean both greater empathy and quicker overstimulation.
Crossed arms don't always signal defensiveness — they're just as often a sign of physical comfort or cold temperature.
A genuine smile engages the muscles around the eyes, not just the mouth, a distinction known as the Duchenne smile.
People tend to unconsciously point their feet toward whoever or whatever holds their interest in a conversation.
Mirroring another person's posture or gestures during conversation often signals rapport and subconscious comfort.
A firm handshake is consistently rated as more trustworthy and competent than a weak one, across multiple cultures.
Prolonged eye contact can signal confidence, but too much without breaks can come across as intimidating rather than engaged.
Touching the face or neck during conversation is often associated with discomfort or mild anxiety, though context matters.
Open, expansive posture is linked not just to appearing more confident, but to actually feeling more confident afterward.
People subconsciously lean toward things and people they like, and lean away from those that make them uncomfortable.
A slight head tilt during conversation is widely read as a sign of active listening and interest.
Micro-expressions, fleeting facial expressions lasting a fraction of a second, can reveal emotions a person is trying to conceal.
Pupils tend to dilate slightly when someone is interested or attracted, a response that's largely involuntary.
Fidgeting can sometimes reflect excitement rather than nervousness, depending on the surrounding context.
People often unconsciously synchronize their walking pace and breathing rhythm with someone they feel connected to.
A relaxed, open palm gesture during conversation is generally perceived as more trustworthy than a closed fist or pointed finger.
An estimated large majority of daily decisions are driven by automatic, subconscious processing rather than deliberate conscious thought.
The brain can process and react to visual information before a person becomes consciously aware they've seen it.
Priming, being subtly exposed to a word or image, can measurably influence unrelated decisions made shortly afterward.
Gut instincts often reflect the brain rapidly processing patterns from past experience, even when the reasoning isn't consciously accessible.
Repeated exposure to an idea, even a false one, can make it feel more true simply through familiarity, a pattern called the illusory truth effect.
The subconscious mind continues processing unsolved problems in the background, which is part of why solutions often appear during unrelated activities.
Scent is one of the most powerful subconscious memory triggers, often evoking emotional memories faster than sound or sight.
People often justify decisions after the fact with logical reasons, even when the real decision was made emotionally and subconsciously.
The brain forms first impressions of trustworthiness from a face in well under a second, long before conscious evaluation kicks in.
Background music tempo can subconsciously influence how fast people walk, eat, or even shop.
Color choices in branding and design tap into subconscious emotional associations that vary by culture and personal history.
The brain edits out minor inconsistencies in visual scenes without conscious awareness, a process linked to change blindness.
Subtle cues like a person's name or a shared birthday can subconsciously increase feelings of connection and trust toward them.
The brain assigns emotional weight to memories in ways that shape future decisions, even when the memory itself isn't consciously recalled.
Dreams are thought to reflect the brain processing and consolidating emotional experiences from waking life.
People tend to attribute their own failures to circumstances but attribute others' failures to their character, a pattern called the fundamental attribution error.
Groups often make riskier decisions collectively than any individual member would make alone.
People are more likely to obey an authority figure's instructions than most predict they would be, even when the instructions conflict with personal values.
Wearing a uniform or shared symbol can measurably increase feelings of group belonging and cooperative behavior.
People judge strangers' competence and warmth within seconds of meeting them, and these first impressions are surprisingly hard to reverse.
In-group bias leads people to favor members of their own group over outsiders, even when group membership is randomly assigned.
Public commitments to a goal, like announcing it to friends, tend to increase follow-through compared to keeping the goal private.
Social exclusion activates some of the same brain regions as physical pain.
People are more likely to donate or help when they can picture a specific individual in need rather than a large, faceless group.
Cultural background shapes how directly people express disagreement, with some cultures favoring explicit confrontation and others favoring indirect cues.
Scarcity, believing something is limited or about to run out, reliably increases how much people want it.
Social proof, seeing others do something, is one of the strongest predictors of whether a person will do the same thing.
People tend to remember unfinished tasks better than completed ones, a pattern known as the Zeigarnik effect.
Simply anticipating a social interaction with a stranger can trigger measurable anxiety, even in people who describe themselves as generally confident.
Anonymity in group settings can reduce individual accountability, a shift known as deindividuation, sometimes leading to behavior a person wouldn't show alone.
Habits form more reliably when tied to an existing routine cue than when relying on willpower alone.
Intrinsic motivation, doing something because it's inherently satisfying, tends to sustain effort longer than external rewards alone.
The brain releases dopamine in response to progress toward a goal, not just upon reaching it, which is why tracking small wins helps motivation.
Breaking a large goal into smaller, specific steps consistently increases the likelihood of follow-through compared to vague intentions.
Environmental design, like keeping healthy snacks visible, often shapes behavior more reliably than relying on self-discipline.
Motivation tends to follow action more often than it precedes it — starting a task, even briefly, often builds the drive to continue.
People are more likely to stick with a habit when it's linked to identity, such as thinking 'I am a runner' rather than 'I want to run.'
Willpower behaves more like a limited daily resource than a fixed trait, which is part of why decisions get harder later in the day.
Immediate rewards are far more motivating to the brain than distant ones, even when the distant reward is objectively larger.
Accountability to another person significantly increases the odds of sticking with a new habit compared to a private, unshared goal.
Procrastination is often driven more by emotional avoidance than by poor time management.
Repeating a behavior in a consistent context speeds up habit formation more than repeating it in varying contexts.
Visualizing the process of achieving a goal tends to be more motivating than visualizing the end result alone.
Small, consistent effort tends to build lasting habits more effectively than occasional bursts of intense effort.
People are more motivated by the fear of losing something than by the prospect of gaining something of equal value, a pattern known as loss aversion.
Information is remembered better when it's spaced out over multiple sessions rather than crammed into one, a pattern called the spacing effect.
Testing yourself on material strengthens memory more effectively than simply re-reading it, a pattern known as the testing effect.
People tend to remember the first and last items in a list better than the ones in the middle, known as the primacy and recency effects.
Memories are not stored like video recordings — they're reconstructed each time they're recalled, which is why they can shift slightly over time.
Emotionally charged events tend to be remembered more vividly and for longer than neutral ones.
Explaining a concept to someone else, or even to yourself out loud, strengthens understanding more than passive review.
Physical movement and gesture during learning can improve recall compared to sitting completely still.
Confidently misremembering an event, called a false memory, can feel just as real to a person as an accurate one.
Learning in the same physical environment where information will later be recalled can improve retrieval, a pattern called context-dependent memory.
Sleep immediately after learning something new significantly improves how well it's retained the next day.
Chunking, grouping information into smaller units, allows people to remember far more than trying to hold individual items in mind.
Multitasking while studying, like texting, has been shown to significantly reduce how much information is retained.
Handwriting notes tends to improve recall compared to typing them, likely because it requires more active processing of the information.
The brain forgets most new information within the first day unless it's reviewed, a pattern described by the forgetting curve.
Curiosity itself enhances memory formation — people remember answers better when they were curious about the question beforehand.
